summary: Source-anchored research for Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Reduce memory demands by making process position and instructions visible: COGA recommends showing completed, current and pending steps, while Coforma recommends persistent instructions throughout multi-step processes. (medium confidence)

COGA recommends authentication alternatives that do not require memorizing strings, calculations, copying content, puzzles, reproducing gestures, or transcribing displayed characters; these are design recommendations, not a claim that every authentication mechanism must have identical cognitive demands. (low confidence)

COGA recommends avoiding timeouts and letting users save work as they go. If that is impossible, explain the available time and whether a timeout will discard entered data when the process begins. (low confidence)
Use clear, concrete language and examples; keep content concise without losing precision. Both COGA and the AASPIRE guidelines recommend this approach. (medium confidence)

Use COGA alongside WCAG to address cognitive usability needs beyond conformance; W3C explicitly describes COGA patterns as supplemental guidance, and DWP recommends cross-referencing them when improving services beyond AA. (medium confidence)

Limit interruptions and distracting motion, and provide user controls: COGA recommends control over interruptions and content changes, and AASPIRE recommends avoiding moving images and decorative visual or sonic clutter. (medium confidence)

Fable cautions that automated checks cannot determine whether language is confusing, steps feel overwhelming or navigation is predictable; its article recommends validation by people with lived cognitive-accessibility experience. (low confidence)

DWP cautions against treating blanket AAA conformance as a universal solution, noting that some content cannot satisfy every AAA criterion; its recommended approach is to consider useful AAA criteria and cross-reference COGA patterns and user stories. (low confidence)

To support task preparation and planning, COGA recommends stating the expected effort, required resources and process overview before a multi-step task, and making in-progress versus completed status clear. (low confidence)

Provide presentation choices rather than assume one display suits everyone: COGA recommends font, spacing and contrast preferences, and AASPIRE recommends color-palette choices and both smaller and larger fonts. (medium confidence)

AASPIRE developed its guidelines through iterative autistic end-user involvement and empirically evaluated the resulting website; this is evidence about that intervention rather than proof that every recommendation works for every neurodivergent user. (low confidence)

In Fable’s pilot, some participants needed to complete tasks silently before explaining their thoughts, so its authors recommend offering a do-first option rather than requiring concurrent think-aloud; this is a pilot-specific observation, not a general incapacity attributed to neurodivergent users. (low confidence)

Design around functional needs rather than assuming a diagnosis determines a person’s interface needs. Fable recommends a needs-based approach, including people without formal diagnoses; W3C identifies memory, attention, processing, language, and learning barriers as distinct design concerns. (medium confidence)
W3C COGA Content Usable provides supplemental guidance beyond WCAG requirements; following it is not required for WCAG conformance. (low confidence)
COGA recommends placing clear, concise instructions before or beside the activity, breaking them into complete steps, and supplying examples or illustrations. (low confidence)

COGA recommends reducing unnecessary decisions and steps: keep required workflows to their minimally necessary steps and separate optional actions, to reduce distractions, mistakes, and mental fatigue. (low confidence)
COGA recommends that context, functionality and settings changes be user initiated or have an easy off switch, together with an easy way to return to the previous state. (low confidence)

Scope AASPIRE findings to their study context: the authors identify a simple informational website, a convenience evaluation sample, and primarily non-Hispanic white participants as limits. (low confidence)

COGA recommends making the page purpose and position within a task recognizable, including after a user loses focus. Its user stories explicitly connect these orientation needs with attention, memory, and executive-function impairments. (low confidence)

COGA recommends an easy way to control interruptions, reminders, and changing content, except user-initiated events or emergencies; it describes pause controls and user-selected interruption settings as attention and memory supports. (low confidence)

COGA recommends supporting personalization and simplification without disabling add-ons or extensions, including spelling support, password support, text-to-speech, and synchronized highlighting. It also recommends user-initiated context changes or an easy off switch, plus a way back to the previous context. (low confidence)
